paragraphs.text: THE TREATISE ON THE MYSTERIES OF SAINT HILARY, BISHOP
BOOK ONE

Manifold [?] … let us understand those very things in the events themselves. For them, however, it is enough to have fitted on some appearance of an empty likeness. A true comparison, though, must be completed in full from what follows and sought on solid ground from what is present.

Every work contained in the sacred books announces in words, expresses in deeds and confirms by examples the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. In that coming he was sent by the Father and was born a man of the Virgin through the Spirit.

For throughout the whole time of this world's existence, by true and perfect prefigurations in the patriarchs, he begets the Church, or washes it, or sanctifies it, or chooses it, or sets it apart, or redeems it: by the sleep of Adam, by the flood of Noah, by the blessing of Melchizedek, by the justification of Abraham, by the birth of Isaac, by the servitude of Jacob.

In short, throughout all time the whole of prophecy, the working out of the mystery, has been granted so that the flesh he was to assume might be known. In this little book I have decided to show that in each and every man, time and event, his coming, his preaching, his passion, his resurrection and our gathering together are displayed beforehand, like an image in a mirror. So I will not mention anything merely in passing. Rather, I will treat everything in its proper time, beginning with Adam, from whom we are given knowledge of the human race. In this way it may be recognized that what was fulfilled in the Lord had been prefigured in many things from the very beginning of the world.
ON ADAM
Adam prefigures the Lord's birth by his very name. For in the Hebrew language 'Adam', which in Greek is 'gē pyrra', that is

in Latin, is 'fiery earth'. And Scripture usually calls the flesh of the human body 'earth'. That flesh was born of the Virgin in the Lord through the Spirit, was changed into a new form foreign to itself, and was made to conform to spiritual glory, as the Apostle says: the second man is from heaven, and the heavenly Adam, because the earthly Adam is the image of the one to come. So, safe in the hands of so great an authority, we also take up the name of Adam not without some reflection on what was to come.

Next, while Adam is cast into sleep, Eve is brought forth from his side and from his bone. When he wakes, a prophecy follows as well: 'This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man, and the two shall be in one flesh.' Here I have no labor, for the Apostle, recalling this very prophecy, says:

'This is a great mystery, but I speak of it in Christ and in the Church.' But we read that only a bone was taken from Adam. How, then, is it said, 'flesh of my flesh'? This could indeed be referred to the reliability of the events at hand. The bone taken from his side was made into a woman's body through him who can do all things [?], clothed with flesh. Since the bone was taken from flesh, and once again clothed with flesh came to exist as a body, then just as it is bone from bone, so also it is flesh from flesh. But the Lord in the Gospels, when the Jews tested him about granting a divorce, shows that this was said by himself rather than by Adam. He says: 'Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother, and the two shall be in one flesh?' For these words come right after the words 'flesh of my flesh.'

So the prophecy followed upon what was being accomplished in Adam. The Lord, who made male and female, said these things, namely that bone is from his bone and flesh from his flesh. In doing so he himself spoke through Adam about what had been done entirely in Adam himself. He did not take away the reliability of the events, and he showed that what was being carried out in another prefigured himself.

For the Word was made flesh, and the Church is a member of Christ, born from his side through water and given life through blood. Again, the flesh in which the Word was born, the Word who abides before the ages and is the Son of God, abides in us through the sacrament. Therefore he taught plainly that Adam and Eve contained the figure of himself and of the Church. He signifies that the Church was sanctified after the sleep of his death by communion in his flesh. The same Lord also speaks through the Apostle:

'For Adam did not sin, but the woman sinned and was in transgression. Yet she will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in the faith.' The Church, then, is made up of tax collectors, sinners and Gentiles.

While her second and heavenly Adam alone did not sin, she herself, a sinner, will be saved through bearing children who remain in the faith. It is not right to understand this to mean that the woman has not been redeemed from her sin by the Lord. If it did, she would be baptized for nothing, if she were to be set free instead by the merit of childbearing. Yet not even bearing children will make her safe, since she is not saved unless those she has borne persevere in faith. And I do not know how it could be just for anyone to be made guilty by another's sin or innocent by another's merit.

But comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we shall be safe in holding this view: the Apostle chiefly refers the events of the great mystery in Adam and Eve to Christ and the Church, proclaiming them as already pointing there. And it is right for us to regard these words as spoken by him spiritually, but in such a way that

his statement must be referred no less to his present teaching and to the instruction of those he was admonishing. In the First Epistle to the Corinthians he proclaimed the manifold mercy of God in sanctifying unbelievers through marriage with believers. Here too he taught that a similar sanctification is to be granted through the bearing of children who nevertheless become believers. Just as the partnership of one believer benefited the unbelieving partner through marriage, so the bearing of believing children would come to the aid of unbelievers.
We must also observe in Adam's sleep and in Eve's being given a body the sacrament of the mystery hidden in Christ and in the Church.

For it contains the faith in bodily resurrection and its reasoning. In the creation of the woman, clay is no longer taken up, earth is not shaped into form, and lifeless matter is not stirred into a living soul by God's breath. Instead, flesh grows upon bone, and the flesh

is given the completion of a body, and spiritual vigor follows upon the completion of the body. God declared this order of resurrection through Ezekiel, teaching the power of his might in the things that were to be done. For there everything comes together: flesh is present and the spirit flies in. None of his works is lost to God, for whom even things that did not exist were at hand to complete the body.

And this sacrament, as the Apostle says, was hidden from the ages in God: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body and sharers in his promise in Christ. And Christ, as the same Apostle says, is able to make the body of our lowliness conform to the body of his glory.

So when the heavenly Adam rises after the sleep of his passion, the Church recognizes her own bone and her own flesh. It is no longer created from clay or brought to life by breathing. Instead it grows upon bone and is made complete as a body from a body, as the Spirit flies in. For those who are in Christ will rise after the pattern of Christ. In him the resurrection of all flesh has already been fulfilled, since he himself was born in our flesh with the power of God in which he was begotten by the Father before the ages.

Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, male and female are all one in Christ. The flesh is recognized as being from flesh, the Church is the body of Christ, and the mystery in Adam and Eve is proclaimed as referring to Christ and the Church. Therefore whatever is being prepared for the Church through Christ for the fulfillment of the ages was already completed under Adam and Eve at the beginning of the world.
ON CAIN AND ABEL
After the first prefiguration of Christ and the Church come the deeds of Cain and Abel. In themselves they prefigure the difference

between two peoples, and by their very names and occupations they signify the character and pursuits of each. For Cain was a tiller of the earth and Abel a shepherd of sheep. Each of them offered God a mystical gift from his own produce. But the gifts of Abel are looked upon, while those of Cain are not regarded. Yet the day of the sacrifice and the place were the same. And how can one be in the sight of God, who beholds all things, and the other outside his sight? By this sign we are taught that God's regard is the mark of what pleases him.

And although all things are subject to him, his regard goes only to what is worthy. Yet nothing had been said earlier about Cain's character to make his offering displeasing. But from what followed we understand the providence of God in not accepting the sacrifices of one who was going to attack his brother. For with God the knowledge of what is to come is as certain as a deed already done.

He who was going to kill is unworthy of God's regard, as though he had already killed. Moreover, tilling the earth signifies the works of the flesh, and all the fruit of the flesh lies in vices. God abhors them, and so they drive his regard away from themselves. So no regard is paid to the offering that comes from the labors of the earth. Only the firstlings of the sheep, with their fat, are pleasing. That is, inward fruits and the sacrifices of our own conscience delight him; these, pleasing to him in the firstlings of the sheep, draw the regard of the divine will upon themselves.

For Christ is the firstfruits, the firstborn of creation, the firstborn from the dead, and also the prince of priests, so that he himself may hold first place in all things. He himself is also a sheep, and by his bodily birth one of the sheep. So Abel's sacrifice is already acceptable under the sacrament of the Church, which would afterward offer the sacrifice of the holy body from the firstlings of the sheep.

So the one who displeased envies the one who pleased. And though God had warned him to be still, against God's command the acceptable one is killed by the unacceptable one. The guilty man is questioned so as to bring him to the repentance of confession, but he denies it and adds to his crime. He despairs of resurrection, thinking that [?] by death. But groaning and trembling he is kept for the judgment of sevenfold vengeance, and he is cursed by the whole earth, which received his brother's blood.
The meaning of the name Cain is 'laughter', and of Abel 'weeping'.

Are not the things described above fulfilled in the two peoples? The offering of the younger is pleasing; the Jew envies the Christian. Though the prophets warned him in vain, he burned with rage to murder him.

He does not seek pardon even through confession and repentance, but boldly denies the crime he committed against God. Despairing of the glory of the resurrection, and subjected to the power of foreign rulers once Jerusalem was taken, he is kept, groaning and trembling, for the judgment of vengeance. The very meanings of the names set him apart from the saints, as the Lord says: 'Woe to those who laugh, for they will weep!' and: 'Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted!'

And to teach that everything fits the prefiguration of both peoples, the Lord said: 'Therefore, behold, I am sending you prophets and wise men and scribes. Some of them you will kill in your synagogues, and you will persecute them from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.'

[?] So Abel's blood is required of the people who, after the prefiguration of Cain, persecuted the righteous and are cursed by the earth that opened its mouth to receive the brother's blood. For in the body of Christ, in which are both the apostles and the Church, their whole flesh and posterity took upon itself the blood of all, as they themselves cried out: 'His blood be on us and on our children.'
So the events that took place in Cain were a prefiguration, and the reality

of what was accomplished followed it. Those on whom vengeance for the same guilt has followed cannot be separated from the pattern of the prefiguration. Moreover, in the words, 'If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?' the figure of the future is contained as well as the meaning of the present event.

For nothing pleases God except what is held in common, shared and offered in friendship. So the people that awaits God's promises through the law may offer rightly to God by observing the commandments. Yet it has sinned unless it shares this very law of God, which is a shadow of things to come, with the gathering of the Gentiles.

So by not dividing rightly it will be held guilty of a crime. Cain, envying his brother, had not shared in the grace of the offering that God regarded, and he was made a sinner because he did not divide rightly. By this example, those who are under the law are guilty, even if they use the law rightly, unless they share in the offerings of the faithful from the Gentiles that God has approved.
ON LAMECH

Even in Lamech, events do not take place apart from a figure of the future. He is recorded as the husband of two wives, and to their names is added the name of a third woman, though she was not bound to him in marriage. The same Lamech is also written to have said this: 'Lamech said to his wives Adah and Zillah: Hear my voice, wives of Lamech, give heed to my words: I have killed a man to my wounding and a young man to my bruising. Sevenfold vengeance has been taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven.'

And who is this, more righteous than the righteous Abel, whose death must now be avenged with so much greater a penalty? The name of the slain man is not mentioned. The wound is attributed not to the slain but to the slayer, and the bruise is said to belong to the one who struck rather than to the one struck.

The killing of the young man is announced to the wives. Although the names of three women are included, he speaks only to two. The ungodly man prophesies, and he heaps up vengeance for the murder he committed beyond the punishment of Cain.
These things must not be heard in passing; rather, we must search out in them the figuring of things to come.

Lamech bears the figure of the chief priest, who nailed the Lord to the cross with the consent of Jews and Gentiles alike. For the same Lord was led from the court of the chief priest to Herod, while the people of believers were kept apart from any share in the crime. That is why he boasts of the killing of the young man to two women, as to his partners and wives.

And because he feels no punishment for it, he took upon himself both the wounds and the bruise of the injury and the murder. He also spoke by prophetic prompting. For at that time too the chief priest prophesied without knowing it, as it is written in the Gospels: 'But one of them, named Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them: You know nothing, nor do you understand that it is better for us that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish. He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year, he prophesied.' So everything agrees together in persons, events and outcome, and the reality of the deeds embraces the figure of things to come.

The number in the punishment of Cain and of Lamech is also not recorded without some meaning. According to the prophets, a sevenfold punishment is appointed for the unjust. Peter, on whom the Lord was building the Church as on a living foundation, asks whether he should forgive one who sins against him seven times, according to the law. The Lord answered that he should forgive seventy times seven. By this sign he taught that the punishment for his passion was to be remitted for those who would believe: as far as the vengeance for it had been multiplied, so far in turn would pardon abound.
Then Seth is born, and in him another seed is raised up in place of the slain Abel, as Eve says: 'God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.'

The meaning of the name Seth is 'foundation of faith'. Abel was righteous, and Seth was born in the place of the righteous one. From this we understand that the generation of the saints is always preserved by God and renewed through succession, and that the Church would uphold the faith for believers on the foundation laid in Peter.
ON NOAH

No one can deny that the events concerning Noah are full both of the mighty works of God and of examples of things to come. However dull a mind may be, or however much a will may turn away from understanding the truth, there are nevertheless words and deeds there that draw out a sense of the truth even from the unwilling. And so that the prophetic power may be understood in each of the events, what is to be compared with what

must be briefly set out. Noah prefigures the man whom the Lord assumed from the Virgin. To make this clear from the words of Scripture itself, we must learn what prophecy his father Lamech made about him: 'And Lamech begot a son and called his name Noah, saying: This one will give us rest from our works and from the sorrows of our hands and from the earth which the Lord God has cursed.'

But these words, I think, cannot fit perfectly the Noah of whom the passage speaks. What rest did he bring to the human race, or from what works did he make it cease? On the contrary, under him the whole of mankind is destroyed and the flood is poured out. The earth is given back into that man's sight, and afterward men live amid even graver [?]. And where will rest have been given through Noah? But the one who was to give rest is marked out as having the power to give it.

Moreover, it does not fit human nature, nor do we read it written, nor do we understand from the events themselves, that Noah did any of these things. But Scripture set out very plainly the many things that properly belonged to Noah. He is approved by God; he is found righteous; he is commanded to build the ark; he enters it; he sends out the raven; he both receives the dove and sends it out again; he leaves the ark; he plants a vineyard; drunk from its fruit, he is uncovered; he is mocked by Ham; he is covered by Shem and Japheth; he lays down a curse for one son and an order and measure of blessing for the other two. These things are to be understood as having been done by him.
But a great sacrament of the future is contained in them, and we shall treat each in its proper place, when the time comes to compare events and persons with one another.

So our Lord, the Word made flesh, will be compared with this Noah. He also says in the Gospels: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.'

So he gives rest and grants rest to souls. Because of the coming judgment he shelters his sons, both those begotten and those called sons, in the ark of his teaching and of his Church. He bestows the Holy Spirit, he dies, he is mocked, he rises again, and

he lays down for the human race punishment for what was done wrongly and sanctification for what was done rightly. And when Noah is commanded to enter the ark or to leave it, we must observe the principle of the Church's sanctification. For it is written: 'You shall enter the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives'; and again: 'The Lord God spoke to Noah, saying:

Go out of the ark, you and your wife and your sons and your sons' wives.' For those entering the ark he groups the sexes separately, the men with the man and the women with the woman. He signifies that those who are to enter the Church must be continent, and that afterward each would receive again the enjoyment of his own marriage [?] … when it was sent out three times.
And it is not uncertain what the next sending out prefigures.

For the dove returns with the fruitful leaves of the olive, no longer to be taken in by hand, but flying back. This was fulfilled when the seventy disciples, having received the Holy Spirit, were sent out to preach the gospel and returned rejoicing that the unclean spirits were subject to them. The Holy Spirit was bringing back the fruit of God's mercy, which is signified in the olive,

and also showing that once the disciples later left the Lord, it would have no rest. Yet the dove flew back to Noah with fruit. By this it signified, in its second return, both the fruit of the Holy Spirit in the subjection of the demons and that, as the disciples were leaving the Lord, there was still no rest for it to settle on. But the third sending out and flight prefigures its dwelling within the believer, when the Holy Spirit, once sent, remains forever in the souls of the faithful.

The drunkenness from the fruit of the planted vineyard, in turn, is a figure of the passion. For the Lord brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it; and again: 'The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel.' The cause of the passion lies in the works of his people, whom he transplanted and planted. If anyone thinks that this drunkenness of Noah does not belong to the figure of the Lord's death, he will be refuted by what follows. Besides, the cup that is drunk in the Gospels also signifies the death of the passion.

There were three sons. The father's nakedness is mocked by one and covered by the other two. But though the two covered it with one mind, and the third was cursed, the two still receive different blessings for one and the same deed. These three sons represent the whole of mankind: those living under the law, those justified under grace, and the Gentiles. Of these, the Gentiles mock the Lord's death and the naked body of God, while the two who cover the nakedness stand for the law and grace.
Because Japheth is settled in the dwellings of Shem, he shows the figure of the Gentiles, who were brought to the faith. Shem, on the other hand, plays the part of the people of Israel [?] …
ON ABRAHAM
[?] … Sarah also signifies the Church, and Hagar the synagogue [?] …

And the seed called in Isaac shows Christ. In him too a prefiguration of the passion is set forth: when he is called by his father to be the sacrifice, when he takes up the wood of the sacrifice, and when a ram stands ready to complete the sacrifice. [?] …
In the letter added to Abraham's name there is the number one; in the letter added to Sarah's there is a hundred. And the Saviour, leaving the

ninety-nine on the mountains, went off to look for the one that had strayed. So the number one is added in Abraham's letter. For there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, born of a virgin, and by that one all the crimes of believers have been cleansed. What he was to fulfil through himself, he prefigures in Abraham. Abraham, by the addition of one, is named father of the nations. Christ himself, by taking up the one, is established as father and redeemer of the nations, once the hundredth sheep has been restored to Sarah, that is, to the first-born church of the heavenly Jerusalem. * * *

The householder in the Gospel visited the barren fig tree by coming three times. In the same way, holy mother Church has marked out the Saviour's coming for herself by a yearly return of a set-apart period of three weeks. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost. He came before the law, because through natural understanding it became known what each person ought to do or to follow. He came under the law, because through the examples of the patriarchs and the proclamations of the prophets he confirmed the decrees of the law to the seed of Abraham. He came a third time, after the law, through grace, to call the Gentiles, so that from the rising of the sun to its setting children might learn to praise the name of the Lord. And he does not stop urging them to the worship of his majesty until the end of the world. * * *
ON ISAAC.

* * * Rebecca bears a twofold figure, of marriage and of childbirth. In her marriage she shows a type of the Church. She gives drink to the camels, that is, to the nations made subject to Christ. Through the earrings she teaches the hearing of faith. The bracelets on her hands show the adornment of good works. When she is asked about the marriage, she answers as those who are to be joined to Christ answer, so that she may come to see him. She goes out from her father's house, showing that unless someone renounces vices and lusts he cannot be Christ's servant. She signifies two nations, two peoples. * * *
ON JACOB.
* * * with Scripture explaining the proper meaning of this name. And Esau said to Jacob: Let me taste some of this red stew, for I am faint.
That is why his name was called Edom. Then he sold his birthright for food, saying: Look, I am dying; what use is this birthright to me? Among the ancients the dignity of the birthright was this:

the firstborn received the inheritance of his father's house, and the brothers born after him were subject to him. For those living in the body, then, the dignity of the firstborn has to do with this life. Esau, prefiguring the unbelieving people, was selling it for fleshly desires. But when he said: Look, I am dying; what use is this birthright to me?, he was certainly not despairing of the present honour of the firstborn, for that primacy, which belongs to human beings, was received before death. Rather, he bore in himself the figure of the people. He was himself the firstborn through the law, for this people had been chosen first to be God's inheritance. Yet he fell from the hope of the resurrection and of God's glory, and, taken up with the desires of the body, he declared that he had given up hope of his honour, the honour that a firstborn ought to hope for after death.
So, with Esau despairing of his birthright, everything else is carried out both according to the reality of the event and according to the force of the prefiguration.

Isaac, then, since his eyes were dim, tells Esau, as was the custom, to prepare him food from his hunting and to be blessed by him before the time of his death. When Rebecca learned of this, she urged Jacob to prepare food for his father quickly from two kids, to put on Esau's robe,

and, since he was smooth, to disguise his hands and his neck by binding the skins of the kids onto them. Having done this, he snatched the blessing that had been prepared for Esau. Then he is blessed with these words: See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed. May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven above, and from the richness of the earth an abundance of grain and wine. Let nations serve you, and princes will bow down to you. Be lord over your brother, and your father's sons will bow down to you. Whoever curses you will be cursed, and whoever blesses you will be blessed.

The event is indeed carried out according to its immediate outcome in Esau and Jacob, but the spiritual prefiguration keeps its own order. The elder had sold his birthright through the desires of the body, giving up hope of the honour of things to come for the sake of present luxury. The younger bought it at the cost of present things.

Do not things to be done spiritually follow upon things done bodily? Unbelievers think that every good lies in pleasure, and the earlier people lost the honour of the resurrection through the desires of the flesh. Believers, however, renounce present joys and place all their hope in things to come. For the sake of that hope they keep themselves restrained in mind and body, and so they snatch away what was meant for the elder.

For Jacob is clothed in Esau's robe, and the robe is regularly mentioned as the garment of immortality, even in the Gospel, where the younger brother, who had also squandered the inheritance he received, received the best robe. And because he was to be brought out of sins into the brightness of innocence, Jacob is covered with the skins of kids, in actual fact so as to imitate his brother's appearance. But because he was to pass from being a sinner to holding the dignity of the blessing he had seized, he takes on the form of a sinner in the skins of dead animals.
The very logic of the blessing and the force of its words show that nothing in it is to be understood according to what happened at the time.
For Jacob is blessed so that from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth he may abound in wine and wheat. Yet in fact he was endangered by famine and bought grain

from Egypt. Nations are made subject to him in servitude; on the contrary, he himself, with his whole household, gave himself into Pharaoh's power. He is said to be one whom princes will bow down to; rather, he endured a long servitude under Laban as his master.

He is made lord over his brother; yet why did he bow down to his brother as to a lord? Scripture runs no risk of falsehood. Therefore, although these things were said of Jacob, they are signified and fulfilled in the people he prefigured. For all these things, according to the promises of the prophets and the Gospel, are kept in store for the faithful, who are to judge the world and the angels and are destined to share in the heavenly kingdom.
Finally, the very opening of the blessing embraces things that are not present but future and perfected. For he says: See,

the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which God has blessed. The smell is the Spirit's foreknowledge; the full field is the perfection of fruits. And, as the Gospels teach, the field stands for the world. But the blessed world must surely be taken to mean not the world that

will be dissolved and will cease to be, but the one that is eternal and full of perfect fruits. Jacob's smell, then, is the same as that of the full field. In the nature of things, smell stands for the Spirit's foreknowledge, since what each thing is can be perceived by smelling it. So Isaac indicates that he smells, that is, foreknows by the Spirit, this blessing of the younger people, a blessing that will belong to the eternal age, with both of them eternal: the age itself and those who will enjoy it.
So that we might see God's abundant mercy in foreshadowing future outcomes under present events, everything was set out and written so care-

fully that one and the same sequence of the narrative fits both the event itself and the future hope. When Isaac was about to bless Jacob in Esau's place, he was anxious not to be deceived in any way, for Esau [?] said that he was Jacob [?]. Since Isaac was blind, he said: Come near to me, my son, and I will feel you, to see whether you are my son Esau or not.

And although he was [?] clothed in Esau's robe and had counterfeited Esau's appearance by putting on the skins, the blind man still felt him over with some suspicion. For as he felt him he said: The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau. These details show that Isaac was anxious out of affection for Esau.

Afterwards Esau returned from the field and the hunt and presented himself to his father as the firstborn, so that he might bless him. When Isaac found out that the blessing had been snatched away, he was not moved. Instead he stood by the blessing he had given, saying: If I have made him your lord and made all his brothers his servants, and have strengthened him with grain and wine, what then shall I do for you, my son?

And when Esau begged him with weeping and tears to bless him, he said this: See, your dwelling will be from the richness of the earth and from the dew of heaven above. You will live by your sword, and you will serve your brother. But it will come about, when you have thrown off his yoke from your neck.

Where, then, does this change of will come from? Why are the man's feelings at odds with each other, unless because the language of Scripture is adjusted both to the accomplishing of events and to the expectation of hope? His anxious questioning came from a father's affection; his refusal to change the blessing came from spiritual knowledge.

In the first he acted according to nature; in the second he kept to the order of prefiguration. In the first he is anxious as a father about sanctifying his firstborn; in the second he holds firm in the spirit of a prophet in blessing the younger people.

The history tells the actual event, and its own sequence does not abandon the hope it prefigures. Yet even here the prophetic plan did not stop short: the sinner, the earlier people, could also hope for the blessing of the younger people, if it believed.

For the way to salvation is open to all, and the road of life is difficult not because of any hardships of its own, since it has none, but because of the right of our own choice. In obtaining God's mercy, the delay lies with the human will, as this very passage about Esau makes clear. He had asked to be blessed, but his father, moved by a spiritual impulse,

left him to the world, gave him over to the sword and consigned him to servitude to his brother. But so that these things should not be thought to have been decreed forever, with no way back through repentance, he put off the blessing Esau was asking for until the time when he should throw off from his neck the yoke of the brother who would rule him. So it is left in his own power to throw off the yoke. For everyone has the free right of their own will to come to faith, and is worthy of the blessing at the point when they have moved from the slavery of irreligion into the freedom of faith.
ON MOSES.

The account of what Moses did also kept to the order of prefiguration that had already begun with Adam. And it is worthy of God's mercy that the deeds of all his patriarchs should, to some extent, imitate the per-

fection of what was to be accomplished in our Lord. For the things fulfilled in him alone and through him alone are prefigured in someone or other through types, times and generations. The imitation of so many ages could not attain the truth that is in him alone. Yet nothing was done in individuals or through individuals without the very imitation in those present deeds almost speaking of what was later accomplished either by him or in him.
Moses was born at the time when Pharaoh had ordered all male

children to be killed at birth. Floating on the water by means of wood, he is preserved to be the people's leader. At the time when our Lord was born as a man, did not the same hatred and fear of a king blaze up against that same man whom he took up for our sake, who

through the sacrament of wood and water was appointed in himself and for himself to heavenly glory and established as king of the nations? Then Pharaoh's daughter, who had come to the river to bathe, took up this Moses. His sister, who was there, offered to find a nurse from among the Hebrews. She then brought his mother, who took him to nurse and brought him back to Pharaoh's daughter, and she received him and adopted him as her son.

Put the persons side by side, compare the outcomes, look at the deeds, and you will find the truth of what followed in the imitation of present events. In Moses' sister, the law followed Christ as far as the sacrament of wood and water. In Pharaoh's daughter is the figure of the nations, for she,

although, as the history truly says, she saw a little child, yet by the event itself kept the force of prophecy. For the law presented the synagogue as both nurse and mother of the infant to the Church, as to Pharaoh's daughter, and so the spiritual order was preserved in the events. As the law itself teaches, it was fitting that Christ be nourished according to the flesh by the one, and adopted by the other.

When Moses had grown up, he went looking for his brothers who were held in slavery. Then he struck down the Egyptian who was lording it over them and mistreating one of them. Afterwards he is rebuked by the very man he had avenged on the Egyptian. Did not Christ, when he had reached full and perfect age, visit his people, who are his brothers according to the flesh? For he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Did he not strike down and conquer the devil who was lording it over them?

For no one will plunder the strong man's goods unless he first binds the strong man. Was he not rebuked by the very people to whom he was giving both vengeance on the devil and freedom from slavery? So what was an imitation in the giver of the law reaches its fulfilment in the God of grace.

The bush burns before Moses' eyes and yet is not consumed. This is the Church, set ablaze by the flames of sins, persecutions and temptations, as the Apostle says: We endure distress and bear want, yet we are not forsaken; we are struck down, yet we do not perish, always carrying about in our body the sufferings of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be
revealed in our body. So the fires of every kind of wickedness rage against us, yet do not burn us up.
Next a sign of faith is given: the rod changed into a serpent, and the serpent done away with and changed back into a rod.

But this change is meant to confirm faith, not to alter nature. The rod stands for the power of kingship, and the serpent is a name for the devil. So we are urged to believe in him who, though he was God of the ages, was thought to be Beelzebul, and who, after being called and thought Beelzebul, was through

the change of the resurrection recognized as God of the ages, which is what he was. The next sign fulfilled the faith of this matter in the form of an imitation, satisfying both hope and time. When the hand placed in the bosom became white as snow, it signified that we who rest in the bosom of the fathers, that is, of Abraham,

Isaac and Jacob, are to be filled with light, the nature of our body being swallowed up into the form of glory and honour. But when the hand, placed in the bosom again, is brought back to what it had been, it teaches that what was prefigured in the sign has not yet come in time. And when, in the third sign, water taken from the river and poured on the ground became blood, the meaning of the sacrament is mingled in, since those washed through water are to pass on to the knowledge of the blood.

It is a great thing that the outcome of events is so contained in what was done under the patriarchs that nothing in it disagrees with what was later fulfilled in the Lord, whether in place, time or reason. For in this the imitation that went before attains the form of the abso-

lute truth and is compared, as an image, to the form it emulates. The deeds were indeed true in themselves, for they took place as bodily realities. But that very truth of human actions was an imitation of divine working. And it happened in this way for the true instruction of our hope and faith, since nothing would be found in the things of God that had not been seen beforehand, as if rehearsed, in the very ages, characters and deeds of human beings.

All the preceding discussion has shown that, up to the people's departure from Egypt, the deeds of Moses agree with what was done either in the Lord or through the Lord. Yet even now a spiritual imitation is joined to bodily truth.

In the desert the people were thirsty. The water is bitter; there is grumbling against the leader. A piece of wood is pointed out, and when it is dipped in, the water is made sweet. And there justification, judgments and testing are decreed.

From there they come to twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camp by the waters. The zeal of opponents may turn their minds aside, and the error of unbelievers may shut off their understanding with the barrier of disobedience, yet they will not be able to ignore the power of so great a work.

For what weight did a piece of wood have in itself, or what power did lifeless matter hold, that it could abolish bitterness, produce sweetness, and both bring in one nature and take away another, so that what had been shunned as harsh now tasted sweet?

What was done at the time does show the working of God's power, transferring nature from one thing into another. Yet we must not think that he needed the help of the wood, as if he could change the waters only through its intervention.

But because God could do all things, he set in motion in the present a secret of his working that was reserved for later times. For the people staying in the desert the water was useless. And indeed we find that peoples are often called waters, as when it is said: The waters saw you, O God, and were afraid; and again: All you waters, clap your hands.

So, whether it was the waters, bitter by their nature, or the whole people staying in the desert, not yet about to gain the promised land and made bitter by grumbling born of stubbornness, either is made sweet by the sacrament of the wood. And it not only stops being what it was, but is changed for the better, beyond what was needed; for it did not merely stop being bitter
but was made sweet. So the wood both acts on the water at hand and, by the sacrament of its power, benefits the peoples who are called by the name of water.

On this wood, in the same Moses, the life of all hangs, when he says: You will see your life hanging before your eyes night and day, and you will be afraid and will not believe in your life. In Jeremiah this wood is put into bread, as follows: They plotted a plot against me, saying:

Come, let us put wood into his bread. From this material comes the rod that overcomes the magicians, terrifies Pharaoh, crushes Egypt, divides the sea, pours the deep back, draws out a spring, takes away bitterness and gives sweetness. By its sacrament

the hearts of unbelievers are softened and brought over from the bitterness of sins and impiety to the sweetness of faith. And so that everything that was done then should fit the effects of the hidden sacrament, Scripture added: There God set justifications and judgments, and there he tested him. When it says 'there', it indicates not a place but an act. For we do not find that any ordinances of justifications, judgments and testings were established in that place.

On the contrary, in the sacrament of the wood on which the Lord hung, and to which he fastened with himself everything that stood against the salvation of the human race, there is justification, because the just man is of faith; there are judgments, because whoever does not believe is already judged; and there is testing, because salvation comes through the stumbling block of the cross.

For the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who believe it is the power of God for salvation. The disgrace of the cross is a testing of faith, unbelief is the cause of judgment, and faith is what earns justification. So it is right that the sacrament of the wood, which turns water from bitterness to sweetness, should contain justification, judgments and testing. And they came to Elim, and there were twelve springs of water there and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters. So the spiritual plan is brought to completion in the course of events. From Marah, the place of bitterness, they come to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. After the knowledge of the sacrament of the wood, that is, of the apostolic and gospel preaching, a place to settle is sought. The seventy preachers give shade for a time, and the twelve apostles flow forever. The seventy chosen preachers of the gospel were later found to be unbelievers, even though they had reported the fruit of faith when the unclean spirits were made subject to them, while the apostles persevered in preaching the faith. So, although seventy trees are mentioned along with twelve springs, yet according to the faithful account of Scripture they rest at the place of the waters alone.

Now how great and how complete is the spiritual meaning in the flesh of the quails and the food of manna! The people who had been led out of Egypt grumble against their leaders and long for the meat they used to eat in Egypt. A flock of quails flies in at evening and covers the camp, and the people are fed with their flesh. In the morning manna is found.

Without distinction of age or sex, the same measure is assigned to each: whoever gathers more has nothing left over, and whoever stores less does not go short. Worms bred in whatever was beyond need. And what was left of the manna in the field melted away as the sun grew hot.

On the sixth day a double portion is stored and does not spoil. On the seventh day there is no manna, though some wait for it in vain. Finally, the omer assigned to each person is stored in a golden vessel and kept as a testimony for future generations.

We must also consider that the manna is given as a test: by keeping its rules each person would be proved whether he was fit for God's commandments. For it is written thus: The Lord said to Moses: Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather each
day's portion day by day, that I may test them whether they will walk in my law or not. But of the meat it was said thus: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled

with bread. The eating in the evening is signified in the meat, and the filling in the morning in the manna. So what concerns the meat is this: the people, staying in the desert, are held back by longing for what they were used to; for they long for the meats of Egypt. They take it toward evening, being, that is, unfaithful to God and impatient of his promises until the consumma-

tion of the age, which is signified by the evening, and taking it in the desires of the world, which is often signified by Egypt. Indeed, the people had this meat only once, so that they might learn it was given not for necessary use but to carry the meaning of a prefiguration. But in the manna there is a test; for through it the people are tested whether they will be obedient to God, that is, whether they will be worthy to receive the true bread from heaven, and the reason for this test must be sought from what follows.

It is found in the morning; for this, in the Lord's resurrection, is the time of the heavenly food. The same amount is appointed for every age and sex. By human nature this is contrary—for when does a little child need as much food as a grown man?—but by spiritual prefiguration it is entirely fitting, since the heavenly food is shared equally among all and its power is not divided by the portions (for we speak of a sacrament to those who know). No one among the greater had too much, nor did

anyone among the least lack; all, that is, were equally filled from what was received divided into portions. As for what was gathered beyond measure and was left over in the morning, turning to worms and stench, there is no doubt that for those who have gathered unnecessary things beyond the heavenly gift and spiritual teaching, these things are both foul in sense, that is, corrupted away from the truth, and seething with the vices of demons, that is, restless with worms; and they are one day to be melted away into liquid when the sun grows hot, that is, when Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, returns for judgment.

In the double gathering of manna on the sixth day for the sake of the seventh day's rest, we are admonished to make an abundant preparation of spiritual works, so that we may use the good things we have prepared then, when the rest has come. Accordingly, what remains from the sixth day does not spoil, whereas what is beyond the measure on the other days stinks.

So too, whatever goes beyond what is prescribed has corruption in store for it in advance. In this time of our age, then, we must work for what we can use in the rest. And this is the time of the six-thousandth year, which is signified by the number of the sixth day, as the prophet says: For a thousand years in the sight of the Lord are as one day.

So on the seventh day, that is, in the Lord's rest, the people are fed on food stored the day before and use what they had prepared, since on the seventh day they would find nothing to feed on; many went out into the field and found nothing. This means that when the times of the ages are closed, we shall find nothing else for the use of our rest except what we have prepared and stored beforehand.

Next, an omer of manna is ordered to be kept in a golden vessel before the Lord for generations to come. But where, pray, is this vessel, and where is the manna that was stored, after the people's many captivities? After the twofold destruction of the city and the temple, what was laid up no longer exists. What then?

Are we to suppose that God did not know manna could not be kept for generations? Surely he who foresees even the future plans of men is not to be thought ignorant of this. Rather, through the figure of the golden vessel, and of the manna stored in God's sight and kept for future generations, he showed that whoever would keep the manna he had received in his body as in a golden vessel would be precious and eternal, while God watches over our undefiled keeping of this spiritual food we have received.
BOOK TWO
ON HOSEA
And in the book of the Prophets another word of the Lord to Hosea is read: Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry,

for the land will go whoring away from the Lord. And after much that comes in between, full of cursing against her, and after the birth of Israel and Not-Beloved and Not-My-People, these words are found: On that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky and the creeping things of the earth, and I will break the bow and the sword and war from the land, and I will settle you in hope, and I will betroth you to myself forever. I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and faith, and you shall know the Lord. And on that day, says the Lord, I will answer the heaven, and the heaven will answer the earth, and the earth will answer the grain and the wine and the oil, and they will answer Israel. And I will sow her for myself upon the earth, and I will love Not-Beloved, and I will say to Not-My-People:

You are my people. And in my judgment there is no room for hesitation: we must understand here a prefiguration of the Church, since the Apostle thought that what had been said above to Hosea about the children of this harlot should be referred to the people of the faithful, when he says to the Corinthians: He has called us not only from the Jews but also from the nations, as he says also in Hosea: I will call Not-My-People My-People, and Not-Beloved Beloved. And in the place where they are called Not-My-People, there they shall be called sons of the living God.

What was done bodily in the prophet, then—that is, the marriage and the begetting (for three were born of the harlot: the first was named Israel by God's command, the next, a daughter, was called Beloved, and the third was called Not-My-People)—this is by God both confirmed and carried out for spiritual understanding.

For this harlot joined to the prophet the Lord made his own bride in righteousness and faith, making a covenant with the beasts of the field, that is, with men made savage by the law of the world; and with the birds of the sky, namely those living in the emptiness and vanity of this world; and with the creeping things of the earth, namely those set in the body with a poisoned and deceitful mind. He would break the bow among the serpents, the sword among the birds, and war among the beasts, taming into peace—by the kinds of weapons and the names of the animals—the various impulses of the human mind: the wars of beasts, the darts of flying things, the venoms of serpents.

Again, heaven answering heaven and earth answering earth signifies a difference in number between the one who hears and the one who is heard, yet shows that what hears and what is heard are the same, since heaven hears heaven and earth hears earth; divinity, moreover, is signified in heaven and bodily nature in earth. And because the Lord was born man from God, and we, who are from man, are to be conformed to God, therefore heaven will hear heaven and earth will hear earth.
As for its hearing in the grain and wine and oil—since these, being without

sense, certainly have no sense of hearing—he nevertheless shows that it is he who will hear in them, under the sacrament of anointing and of the body. Through these, as Israel hears, he sowed for himself the harlot betrothed to him in hope, passing over the one who was named Israel and granting to the others the honour of a change, so that what was not his people should be his people, and she who was not beloved should be Beloved.
For Israel, in Abraham his father, was chosen out of the nations, as is said in the Psalms: the house of Jacob from a barbarous people. But lingering in sins and given over to vain religions,

and unfaithful to God's promises, he did not deserve to receive what was promised, and though first chosen to be God's people, he lost the honour of election. For nothing more is said of Israel, born first of the harlot, and God's whole word concerns those born afterward—those who had earlier been rejected and cut off from affection and belonging, born not to be loved, begotten not to be claimed. But first the harlot is chosen as a bride for God, in faith and righteousness; then those not loved, those not his own, those born of the harlot—these are called sons of the living God.

And this word of God, in which the prophet is commanded to take a harlot as his wife, had to be mentioned for this reason: since we are taught that all things are prefigured through the deeds of the Old Testament and are to be accomplished in the Lord and through the Lord, we might understand from the very fact that a harlot is joined to the prophet that the ignorance of the Gentiles is shown to be united with the prophetic teachings, from which those born would be called beloved instead of not beloved, a people instead of no people, sons of God from a harlot mother.
ON JOSHUA SON OF NUN

Now although it was useful to have treated this for understanding the meaning of spiritual events, we have mentioned this passage chiefly for this reason: since we were going to speak of Rahab, in order to show that the Church was prefigured in her, we might safely set down this comparison between the Church and a prostitute as our understanding of the sense, seeing that the harlot joined to the prophet was found to have been betrothed, as a prefiguration of the Church, in the eternal hope of righteousness and faith and knowledge of God.

And indeed the greatest force of the prophecy lies in the fact that everything concerning her was done under Joshua. For in the one given the name Jesus the full meaning of the future sacrament was revealed. After God's long discourse to Moses, when he had been told to make everything on earth according to the pattern he had seen on the mountain, Moses gave the name Jesus to the man formerly called Hoshea, who was to be the leader of the people on their way to the land of promise. Commanded to arrange everything after the pattern of the heavenly vision, Moses added to the future leader the name that had already been prepared in heaven for the eternal leader.

For as this one was ruler of the synagogue, so that one is ruler of the Church. As this one was leader for taking possession of the promised land, so that one is leader into the land to be inherited, of which the Lord says: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.

As this one came after Moses, so that one came after the law. As this one was commanded to circumcise a second time with a stone knife, so by the Lord—who is both the sharp word that pierces even to the dividing of the soul, and the cornerstone—the circumcision of the heart was spiritually renewed. As this one divided the waters, so that one divides peoples; for he says: I have not come to send peace, but division.

As this one brought twelve stones up from the deep onto the land as an eternal witness, and placed others from the land in the deep, so that one both brought forth the apostolic teaching from the synagogue and left it in the synagogue, for it to use even now if it wished; since, as an eternal witness in the twelve stones, the apostolic teaching was both brought out of the law and yet was found in the law.
And how clear and complete is the very division of the waters, when one part stood whole and full, while the other, its bed dried up,

flowed away entirely into the sea, with the ark of the Lord and the priests standing in the middle! By this sign it is understood that part of the people would cease from the course of their sins and of their death at the coming of the ark of God, that is, at his bodily coming, while the rest would flow down into the sea, that is, into the condemnation and fellowship of this world.
Under this Joshua, then, we must consider what was done by Rahab and in Rahab. For two spies, sent to survey

the land, turned aside in the city of Jericho to the house of this prostitute. She takes them in and hides them; when the king demands that she hand them over, she lies that they have gone back. Then, with them hidden in her house, she says she knows that the Lord has delivered everything in her city to them, and that their God is God in heaven above and on earth below.

She begs them to spare her and all her household when the city is taken. The spies promise that whatever was found within her house would remain unharmed, and that anyone who went out of the house would be responsible for his own death; and they set as a sign a scarlet cord

hanging from the window, and report the whole matter to Joshua. Then they approach the city. The priests with the ark of the Lord go around it for six days, and on the seventh day, when they had gone around seven times, the walls of the city fell at the sound of the trumpet; and when all who were in the city had been killed, Rahab alone, with all her household, is spared by Joshua.

This sequence of events is bound up with great sacraments of things to be accomplished spiritually. The prostitute received into her house two spies sent by Joshua: the sinful Church received the law and prophecy, sent to search out the faith of men, through which God is confessed both in heaven above and on earth below. After his spiritual generation she learned of his attested bodily birth; for she learned it in these words: After this he was seen on earth and lived among men.

From the same spies she also received the sign of salvation in scarlet, a colour that is royal in dignity and blood-red as befits the body, both of which meet in the Passion, when the Lord was clothed in such a garment and blood flowed from his side.

Manasseh too received this scarlet as a sign; by this blood the houses marked in Egypt were kept safe, the book of the covenant was sprinkled, and the people was sanctified. And whoever of the household was found outside the house was made responsible for himself, teaching that those who had been outside the Church would be the cause of their own death.
Jericho, set forth as a figure of this world, is circled for six days; on the seventh it falls at the sound of the trumpet, and the house of Rahab is kept intact through Joshua.

For the six days show the time of six thousand years, during which men have wandered around the world and run about in a kind of cycle of generations; this same world is to be dissolved at the sound of the trumpet in the seventh millennium, while the Church alone—through receiving the spies, through confessing God in the body, through the sign of scarlet appointed through Joshua—is to be preserved with all her household.

We have often urged that the reading of the divine Scriptures must be pursued with such diligence that, by careful examination and sound judgment, it can discern when the account of events is to be understood plainly and when typologically. Otherwise, by misusing both without restraint or skill, we would make both useless to our hearers: either the knowledge of the plain sense would be corrupted by empty claims of prefiguration, or the force of the prefigurations would go unrecognized under the assumption of a plain sense. And yet the word of divine Scripture is such that nothing in it is found empty, nothing without the reason of some necessity, nothing set down that does not demand discernment in the understanding we must seek.

For when the creation of the world is recounted, God is known in the act of creating; when we hear that Enoch was taken up, man is understood to be capable of becoming eternal; when Lot is to be spared as the five cities burn, we learn that God cares for the innocent; when his wife, looking back against God's command, is changed into a pillar of salt, we are trained by fear of the example to obey God's ordinances; when the sins of the Amorites are waited on until they are complete, we recognize both God's mercy and his justice, since by his waiting the time for us to cease from sin is extended, and vengeance is decreed to be deferred until the measure of crimes is full.

And then how necessary for knowledge are the order of the generations, the election of Abraham, the begetting of the patriarchs, the slavery of the people, the plagues of the Egyptians, the dividing of the sea, the raining down of manna, the establishing of the law, the distinguishing of sacrifices, the time of the judges, the knowledge of the kingdoms, the deportation of the people into captivity,

the visions of the saints, the admonitions of the prophets! For in all that has been mentioned above, God the Father and God the Son—God the Son from God the Father, God and man, Jesus Christ—is recognized: when in the creation of the world God commands and God accomplishes; when man is formed in the likeness of a shared image; when the Lord rains sulphur and fire from the Lord (for no one would command himself to act, nor would one alone extend his partnership to another, nor would a single person give to himself and receive from himself); when a man is seen by Abraham and God is worshipped; when in Jacob's wrestling with a man God is seen, and he, holding a man, asks to be blessed by the Lord; when, though only three youths had been thrown into the furnace by Nebuchadnezzar, a fourth is seen like the Son of God; when a virgin bears Emmanuel, him who is God with us.

It was fitting, then, that these things, signified by all and known and fulfilled in that one alone, be preserved in memory in written and sealed volumes, so that posterity, instructed by the deeds of earlier times, might both contemplate the present in the past and still revere the past in the present.

For likewise, since the knowledge of truth is perfect when truth is understood through reason—for all things were written for our knowledge and for the firmest faith of our judgment—these things, which were recorded in books by God's decree, did not themselves need to be known by posterity.

Rather, it was posterity that needed knowledge of the Scriptures: to learn the truth, to receive the teaching of truth through reason, to follow the knowledge of life as it advanced, so to speak, from its very cradle; that is, not to doubt that God is from God, since the Lord rained from the Lord; not to be ignorant of the one unbegotten God, since God commanded; not to be unaware of the only-begotten God, since God made; not to doubt that the two are one, since one pattern of a shared image was established in man; not to deny that God into man [?] … [?]

[?] … born to the fathers. And it is easy to hear Paul boasting that he is a Hebrew, an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin. Therefore, since it is Elijah's office to turn the hearts of the fathers to the sons, the mystery of the perfect preaching is reserved for him, so that he may turn the fathers to the faith which the spirit of the same prophecy has already confirmed in the sons.
